items.stem: A 70-year-old right-handed woman is brought in because she ignores food on the left side of her plate and does not dress her left arm. She denies any problem. Which lesion is most likely?
items.explanation: Hemispatial neglect with anosognosia most often follows injury to the right (nondominant) inferior parietal lobule, which directs attention to both sides of space. A left parietal lesion produces Gerstmann or language problems and only mild, transient right neglect. An occipital pole lesion causes a contralateral field cut that patients usually notice. Left prefrontal injury causes abulia or Broca aphasia.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has transverse myelitis. Her sensory level is at the umbilicus, and when she flexes her neck against resistance the umbilicus moves upward. Which cord level is most likely the upper margin of the lesion?
items.explanation: The umbilicus is supplied by the T10 dermatome. Beevor sign, upward movement of the umbilicus, indicates weakness of the lower abdominal muscles, supplied from T10 to T12, with intact upper abdominal muscles, localizing the lesion near T10. The nipple line is T4, the xiphoid region T7, and the inguinal region L1, none of which matches the umbilical level.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man cannot recognize his wife by sight but identifies her immediately by her voice. Visual acuity and fields are normal, and he recognizes common objects. Which lesion is most likely?
options: Bilateral angular gyri at the parieto-occipital junction
Bilateral superior parietal lobules of the dorsal stream
Bilateral fusiform gyri in the inferior occipitotemporal region
Bilateral calcarine cortex of the primary visual area
items.explanation: Prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces with preserved elementary vision, is typically caused by bilateral, or sometimes right-sided, injury to the fusiform gyri of the ventral visual stream. Bilateral angular lesions produce alexia and agraphia. Injury to the dorsal stream causes optic ataxia and simultanagnosia, and calcarine injury produces cortical blindness. Voice recognition is spared because it uses the auditory pathways.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has an infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Which findings should be expected on examination?
options: Right arm dysmetria with intention tremor and a tendency to fall right
Left arm dysmetria with intention tremor and a tendency to fall left
Bilateral truncal ataxia with normal limb coordination
Right resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia
items.explanation: Cerebellar hemispheres coordinate the ipsilateral limbs, because the cerebellar efferents cross twice, once in the superior peduncle decussation and again in the corticospinal tract. A right hemispheric infarct therefore produces right dysmetria, intention tremor, and falls toward the right. Isolated truncal ataxia is a midline vermis sign. Resting tremor with rigidity belongs to basal ganglia disease.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has a lacunar infarct causing right facial droop, dysarthria, and tongue deviation, with no limb weakness. Which part of the internal capsule is the most likely location?
items.explanation: The genu of the internal capsule carries corticobulbar fibers to the cranial nerve nuclei, so a lacune there produces facial weakness, dysarthria, and tongue deviation without limb weakness. The posterior limb carries corticospinal fibers to the limbs. The anterior limb contains frontopontine and thalamocortical fibers, and the retrolenticular part carries optic radiation and auditory fibers.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has a skull base metastasis. His jaw deviates to the right on opening, his right masseter is weak, and he has numbness of the right lower face and chin. Which foramen is most likely involved?
options: Foramen rotundum transmitting the maxillary division
Foramen ovale transmitting the mandibular division
Superior orbital fissure transmitting the ophthalmic division
Stylomastoid foramen transmitting the facial nerve
items.explanation: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the lower face and motor fibers to the muscles of mastication, and it exits through the foramen ovale. Jaw deviation occurs toward the weak side because of the unopposed contralateral pterygoid. The maxillary division, through the foramen rotundum, is purely sensory over the mid face. The ophthalmic division serves the forehead, and the stylomastoid foramen carries the facial nerve.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a skull base tumor. She has hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, weakness turning her head against resistance on one side, and loss of taste on the posterior tongue. Through which foramen do the affected nerves exit?
items.explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves leave the skull through the jugular foramen, explaining dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of posterior taste, and sternocleidomastoid weakness (Vernet syndrome). The hypoglossal canal carries only the twelfth nerve. The internal acoustic meatus carries the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, and the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and spinal accessory roots. Together these findings point to a skull base lesion rather than a brainstem lesion.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has right facial weakness involving the forehead, inability to abduct the right eye, and left arm and leg weakness sparing the face. Which location best explains these findings?
options: Left caudal pontine tegmentum with the abducens nucleus
Right rostral midbrain with the third nerve fascicle
Right lateral medulla with the nucleus ambiguus
items.explanation: A lower motor neuron facial palsy and an abducens palsy on the same side with contralateral hemiparesis define Millard-Gubler syndrome, from a ventral pontine lesion that damages the fascicles of nerves six and seven and the corticospinal tract before it crosses. A left tegmental lesion would not explain right limb findings. A midbrain lesion affects the oculomotor nerve, and a lateral medullary lesion produces dysphagia and sensory loss.

items.stem: Which central nervous system cell type is derived from mesodermal hematopoietic precursors rather than neuroectoderm, and acts as the resident phagocyte of the brain?
items.explanation: Microglia originate from yolk sac progenitors of mesodermal lineage that colonize the developing brain, and they serve as resident immune cells that phagocytose debris and present antigen. Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells all arise from neuroectoderm. Astrocytes maintain the blood-brain barrier and extracellular potassium, oligodendrocytes form central myelin, and ependymal cells line the ventricles. Their lineage explains why they respond to systemic immune signals.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man develops docility, placidity, hyperorality, and indiscriminate sexual behavior after severe bilateral anterior temporal injury. Which structure is most responsible?
items.explanation: Kluver-Bucy syndrome results from bilateral injury to the amygdala and anterior temporal lobes, removing fear and emotional salience and producing hyperorality, hypersexuality, and visual agnosia. Mammillary body injury produces anterograde amnesia of the Korsakoff type. The dentate gyrus supports memory formation, and orbitofrontal injury causes disinhibition without the placidity and oral exploration. Docility together with hyperorality is the discriminating pairing.

items.stem: A 49-year-old right-handed teacher after a stroke cannot write, cannot do simple arithmetic, cannot name her own fingers, and confuses right with left. Language comprehension is normal. Which area is damaged?
items.explanation: This tetrad of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation is Gerstmann syndrome, localized to the dominant (left) angular gyrus and adjacent inferior parietal lobule. Right-sided injury produces neglect and constructional problems instead. The inferior frontal operculum is the Broca area and produces nonfluent speech. Posterior cingulate injury affects memory and attention networks but not this tetrad.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man treated with risperidone develops breast enlargement and galactorrhea with an elevated serum prolactin. Which pathway is blocked?
items.explanation: Dopamine released from the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus into the portal circulation inhibits prolactin secretion from the pituitary, so D2 blockade by antipsychotics raises prolactin. The nigrostriatal pathway blockade produces parkinsonism. Mesolimbic blockade mediates the antipsychotic effect on positive symptoms, and mesocortical pathway underactivity is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms rather than endocrine changes. Metoclopramide can cause the same effect for the same reason.

items.stem: During caloric testing, cold water is irrigated into the right ear of a comatose-free, cooperative patient with an intact brainstem. In which direction is the fast phase of nystagmus?
items.explanation: Cold irrigation inhibits the ipsilateral vestibular afferents, so the eyes drift slowly toward the cold ear, and the cortex generates a corrective fast phase away from it, to the left. The right-directed fast phase would result from warm irrigation. Vertical nystagmus does not arise from unilateral horizontal canal stimulation. The test exploits the vestibulo-ocular reflex and assesses canal function and brainstem integrity.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has a large right frontal infarct involving the frontal eye field and left hemiparesis. In the first days, where do his eyes rest?
options: Away from the lesion, toward the paralyzed side on the left
Toward the side of the lesion, to the right
items.explanation: Each frontal eye field drives contralateral saccades through the paramedian pontine reticular formation, so an acute destructive lesion leaves the opposite frontal eye field unopposed and the eyes deviate toward the lesion, looking away from the hemiparetic limbs. In pontine lesions the opposite occurs. Downward or upward deviations with eyelid changes belong to dorsal midbrain syndromes, not a hemispheric stroke.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has sudden urinary retention, saddle numbness, and bilateral radicular leg pain with absent ankle reflexes and flaccid leg weakness. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Conus medullaris syndrome with early symmetric sphincter loss
Central cord syndrome with greater arm than leg weakness
Anterior cord syndrome with preserved dorsal column function
items.explanation: Asymmetric radicular pain, areflexia, flaccid weakness, saddle anesthesia, and retention indicate compression of lower motor neuron roots, the cauda equina. Conus lesions tend to have early symmetric sphincter loss, less radicular pain, and sometimes mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs. Central cord injury spares the legs relative to the arms. Anterior cord syndrome produces loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration.

items.stem: A 12-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass develops relentless eating, rapid weight gain, and rage outbursts. Which hypothalamic region is most likely destroyed?
options: Lateral hypothalamic area, which drives feeding and arousal
Suprachiasmatic nucleus, which sets circadian rhythm
Mammillary bodies, which relay hippocampal output
items.explanation: The ventromedial nucleus is the satiety center, and its destruction by craniopharyngioma or surgery causes hyperphagia, obesity, and irritability. Lateral hypothalamic injury does the opposite, producing anorexia and weight loss. The suprachiasmatic nucleus governs sleep-wake timing, and mammillary body damage is linked to memory loss, as in thiamine deficiency, rather than weight gain. Hypothalamic obesity after suprasellar surgery is a recognized complication.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with hypertension develops sudden, violent, flinging movements of his right arm and leg. Which structure is most likely infarcted?
items.explanation: Contralateral hemiballismus localizes to the subthalamic nucleus, which normally excites the internal pallidum; its loss disinhibits the thalamus and produces flinging movements on the opposite side. The right subthalamic nucleus would affect the left limbs. Caudate injury more often causes chorea or behavioral change, and nigral loss produces parkinsonism. The movements often improve gradually over weeks to months.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy with a pineal region tumor cannot look upward, has dilated pupils that react poorly to light but constrict on accommodation, and shows retraction of the eyes on attempted upgaze. Which location is damaged?
options: Pontine tegmentum near the abducens nucleus
items.explanation: Upgaze paralysis, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation, and eyelid retraction make up the dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome, caused by compression of the posterior commissure and pretectal region, classically by pineal tumors or hydrocephalus. Ventral midbrain lesions produce Weber syndrome. Pontine tegmental lesions cause horizontal gaze palsy, and medial medullary lesions spare eye movements. The pupils are classically large with preserved near response.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks of gestation has an elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein level. Which fetal condition should be evaluated first by ultrasound?
items.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein, produced by the fetal liver and yolk sac, leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal blood when the neural tube fails to close, so elevated levels suggest an open defect such as myelomeningocele or anencephaly. Trisomy 21 and trisomy 18 are associated with low maternal levels. Holoprosencephaly is a forebrain cleavage defect with a closed neural tube and does not elevate the marker.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man after a skull base fracture has marked polyuria with dilute urine and rising serum sodium. Which hypothalamic neurons were most likely injured?
options: Arcuate nucleus and its dopaminergic tuberoinfundibular neurons
Medial preoptic area regulating temperature and sexual behavior
items.explanation: Neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei synthesize vasopressin and transport it down the pituitary stalk to the posterior pituitary, so injury produces central diabetes insipidus with dilute urine and hypernatremia. Arcuate injury would raise prolactin. The suprachiasmatic nucleus governs sleep-wake timing, and the preoptic area governs heat loss rather than water balance. Treatment is with desmopressin.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has diplopia on looking left. Her left eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze, with nystagmus in the abducting right eye, and convergence is normal. Which structure is injured?
items.explanation: Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye defines internuclear ophthalmoplegia, named for the side of the weak adduction. Here the left eye fails to adduct, so the left fasciculus is injured. Preserved convergence shows the oculomotor nucleus and nerve work normally, excluding a left nuclear lesion. A right fasciculus lesion would impair right eye adduction.

items.stem: A 68-year-old right-handed man wakes with a right visual field cut. He can write and speak normally and name objects, but cannot read even his own handwriting. Which lesion pattern explains this?
options: Left occipital cortex plus the splenium
Left angular gyrus alone with sparing of the occipital lobe
Right occipital cortex plus the genu of the corpus callosum
Left inferior frontal gyrus with adjacent insular cortex
items.explanation: Alexia without agraphia is a disconnection syndrome. A left posterior cerebral infarct causes right hemianopia, so words are seen only by the right occipital cortex, and damage to the splenium blocks transfer to the left-hemisphere language areas. Writing remains intact because language cortex is spared. An isolated angular lesion would impair writing as well, and frontal lesions produce nonfluent speech.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has a drooping right eyelid with the eye turned down and out, and a dilated pupil, plus left arm and leg weakness and left lower facial weakness. Where is the lesion?
items.explanation: An ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis defines Weber syndrome, from injury to the cerebral peduncle and the exiting third nerve fascicle in the ventral midbrain. The corticospinal fibers have not yet crossed, so weakness is opposite the lesion. A pontine lesion would involve cranial nerves six or seven, and a medullary pyramid lesion spares the eye movements.

items.stem: A newborn weighing 4.8 kg after a difficult shoulder delivery holds the right arm adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended and forearm pronated. Grasp is intact. Which structure is injured?
options: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
Long thoracic nerve in the axilla
items.explanation: Erb palsy follows traction injury to the upper trunk (C5 and C6 roots), weakening shoulder abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion while preserving hand grasp, producing the waiter's tip posture. A lower trunk injury, Klumpke palsy, weakens the hand and may cause Horner syndrome. Posterior cord injury affects the deltoid and extensors, and long thoracic injury causes winged scapula only.

items.stem: An autopsy of a 70-year-old man with severe depression of arousal and mood reveals marked loss of pigmented neurons in the locus coeruleus. Which neurotransmitter is mainly synthesized there?
items.explanation: The locus coeruleus in the dorsolateral pons is the principal source of norepinephrine in the brain, projecting widely to regulate arousal, attention, and mood. Serotonin is produced by the raphe nuclei, dopamine mainly by the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area, and acetylcholine by the nucleus basalis of Meynert and the pedunculopontine nucleus. Loss of locus coeruleus neurons is prominent in Parkinson and Alzheimer disease.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man after a retroperitoneal hematoma has weak hip flexion, weak thigh adduction, weak knee extension, a reduced knee jerk, and numbness over the anterior and medial thigh. Which is the most likely site of injury?
options: Femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
L5 root in the lateral recess
items.explanation: Weakness of hip flexion and knee extension from femoral territory together with thigh adduction from the obturator nerve indicates injury proximal to the nerve divisions, in the lumbar plexus within the psoas, as with retroperitoneal bleeding. A femoral neuropathy would spare adduction. An isolated obturator lesion spares knee extension, and an L5 root lesion causes foot drop.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man undergoing aortic surgery awakens with bilateral leg paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the nipple line. Vibration and proprioception are normal. Which structure is spared?
items.explanation: This is the anterior spinal artery syndrome. The artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord, including the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts and the anterior horns. The posterior columns receive supply from the paired posterior spinal arteries, so vibration and position sense remain intact. Because the paired posterior arteries are rarely affected, the dorsal columns are classically spared in this syndrome.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man has sudden left hemiplegia, left hemisensory loss, and a left homonymous hemianopia without aphasia or neglect. Which artery supplies the structures involved in this classic triad?
items.explanation: The anterior choroidal artery arises from the internal carotid artery and supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic tract and lateral geniculate body, and part of the globus pallidus, so occlusion produces hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, and hemianopia. The recurrent artery of Heubner supplies the caudate head and anterior limb. The communicating arteries give small perforators to the hypothalamus and thalamus.

items.stem: A 57-year-old right-handed man has fluent speech with frequent phonemic errors. His comprehension is good, but he cannot repeat the phrase "no ifs, ands, or buts" and he recognizes his errors with frustration. Which pathway is most likely disrupted?
options: Posterior superior temporal gyrus, the site of auditory word comprehension
Anterior corpus callosum, which joins the two motor cortices
Arcuate fasciculus linking the temporal and frontal language areas
Inferior frontal gyrus, which programs articulation
items.explanation: Fluent speech with intact comprehension and disproportionately poor repetition defines conduction aphasia, caused by interruption of the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke and Broca areas. Damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus would impair comprehension. Callosal lesions produce disconnection apraxia rather than aphasia. An inferior frontal injury would cause effortful, nonfluent speech with relatively spared understanding.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has abrupt coma that improves to severe sleepiness. She has an upward gaze palsy, memory impairment, and apathy. MRI shows symmetric infarcts in the medial diencephalon. Which vascular supply explains the pattern?
options: A single artery of Percheron supplying both paramedian thalami
Bilateral posterior communicating arteries feeding the anterior thalami
Paired anterior choroidal arteries feeding the posterior limb
Bilateral thalamogeniculate arteries feeding the lateral nuclei
items.explanation: Bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarction arises from occlusion of the artery of Percheron, a single trunk from one posterior cerebral artery. It causes hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy, and amnesia from loss of the intralaminar and dorsomedial nuclei. Thalamogeniculate occlusion causes a lateral sensory syndrome. Anterior choroidal infarcts affect the capsule and lateral geniculate body, and polar artery disease affects anterior nuclei.

items.stem: A 64-year-old right-handed man develops slow, effortful, telegraphic speech with preserved comprehension after a stroke. He repeats poorly and has right arm weakness. Which structure is most likely infarcted?
items.explanation: Nonfluent speech with good comprehension and impaired repetition defines Broca aphasia, localized to the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, with adjacent motor cortex explaining the arm weakness. Posterior superior temporal injury produces fluent, empty speech with poor comprehension. Angular gyrus lesions cause alexia with agraphia and Gerstmann features. A right frontal lesion in a right-handed person would produce aprosodia, not aphasia.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has low back pain radiating down the posterior thigh and calf to the lateral foot. He has weak plantar flexion, an absent ankle jerk, and numbness of the lateral foot. Which explanation is most likely?
options: S1 root compression by an L5-S1 disc
L5 root compression by an L4-L5 disc
L4 root compression by an L3-L4 disc
Peroneal nerve compression at the fibular head
items.explanation: The S1 root mediates the ankle jerk, plantar flexion, and sensation over the lateral foot, and a posterolateral L5-S1 disc typically compresses it. L5 compression weakens great toe and ankle dorsiflexion with dorsal foot numbness and a preserved ankle jerk. L4 compression reduces the knee jerk and medial leg sensation. A peroneal neuropathy produces foot drop without reflex changes.

items.stem: A 2-year-old girl has a large head circumference, delayed motor milestones, and ataxia. MRI shows cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle with hypoplasia of the vermis and an elevated tentorium. Which diagnosis fits best?
items.explanation: Vermian hypoplasia with a cystic fourth ventricle and an enlarged posterior fossa with high tentorial insertion defines Dandy-Walker malformation, often with hydrocephalus. Chiari II involves a small posterior fossa, beaked tectum, and myelomeningocele. Chiari I is isolated tonsillar descent through the foramen magnum in older children or adults. Aqueductal stenosis dilates the lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man develops a right superior quadrantanopia and fluent speech with poor comprehension and repetition after a stroke. Which vessel is most likely involved?
options: Superior division of the left middle cerebral artery
Inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery
items.explanation: The inferior division supplies the lateral temporal cortex, including the Wernicke area and the optic radiation fibers of Meyer loop, producing fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension and a contralateral superior quadrantanopia. The superior division supplies frontal regions, producing nonfluent aphasia and contralateral weakness. Posterior cerebral occlusion causes a hemianopia without aphasia, and anterior choroidal occlusion causes capsular hemiplegia.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has right facial paralysis involving the forehead, loss of taste on the anterior tongue, and sound sensitivity in the right ear, but normal tearing. Where is the lesion?
options: Within the internal acoustic meatus before the geniculate ganglion
Within the facial canal between the geniculate ganglion and the stapedius branch
At the stylomastoid foramen after all branches have left
At the cerebellopontine angle with eighth nerve involvement
items.explanation: Hyperacusis arises from stapedius paralysis and loss of anterior tongue taste from chorda tympani involvement, while preserved lacrimation shows that the greater petrosal nerve has already branched off. The lesion therefore lies in the facial canal distal to the geniculate ganglion but proximal to the stapedial branch. Meatal lesions would also reduce tearing. A stylomastoid lesion spares taste and hyperacusis.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has severe headache, seizure, and bilateral thalamic edema on MRI from thrombosis of the vein of Galen. Into which structure does this vein drain?
items.explanation: The internal cerebral veins and basal veins of Rosenthal join to form the great vein of Galen, which unites with the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus, draining to the confluence of sinuses. The superior sagittal sinus drains the convexity and arachnoid granulations. The inferior petrosal sinus connects the cavernous sinus to the jugular bulb, and the cavernous sinus drains the orbit.

items.stem: A 60-year-old right-handed woman has an anterior cerebral artery infarct. The left hand cannot perform commands such as waving goodbye, though it works normally when she imitates or uses objects, and the right hand is normal. Which structure is damaged?
options: Left supramarginal gyrus, the main praxis center
Right primary motor cortex of the arm area
Posterior limb of the left internal capsule
items.explanation: Callosal apraxia occurs when the verbal command, processed in the left hemisphere, cannot reach the right motor association cortex that guides the left hand. Anterior callosal infarcts from anterior cerebral artery disease produce this. A left supramarginal lesion would affect both hands. Right motor cortex or capsular damage would cause weakness rather than isolated command-specific apraxia.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy with a fourth ventricle tumor has severe vertigo, spontaneous nystagmus, and inability to sit or stand without falling, though his limbs are coordinated on bed testing. Which part of the cerebellum is most involved?
items.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe is the vestibulocerebellum, connected to the vestibular nuclei and essential for balance and eye movement control, so injury produces nystagmus, vertigo, and severe truncal instability. The anterior vermis controls leg coordination during gait. Hemispheric lesions cause limb dysmetria, which is absent here. The tonsil is a hemispheric structure whose herniation, not primary injury, is important.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with a facial infection develops ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and numbness over the forehead and cheek from cavernous sinus thrombosis. Which cranial nerve runs freely within the sinus lumen, next to the internal carotid artery, rather than in its lateral wall?
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
items.explanation: The abducens nerve lies in the lumen beside the carotid artery and its sympathetic plexus, so it is often the first nerve affected by sinus thrombosis or an expanding carotid aneurysm. The oculomotor and trochlear nerves and the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve run along the lateral wall, protected by the dural lining. All of them can eventually be involved, producing ophthalmoplegia and facial numbness.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man cannot show how to use a hammer or comb his hair on command, but he uses the objects correctly during daily activities. Strength and sensation are normal. Which lesion is most likely?
options: Left supramarginal gyrus or its connections to the premotor cortex
Right occipital cortex with its ventral stream pathway
Left primary motor cortex for the hand and forearm
Bilateral anterior temporal lobes with amygdala damage
items.explanation: Ideomotor apraxia, impaired performance of learned movements to command despite normal strength, localizes to the dominant inferior parietal lobule, including the supramarginal gyrus, or the pathways relaying praxis plans to premotor cortex. Right occipital injury affects vision. A primary motor lesion would cause weakness. Bilateral temporal injury produces Kluver-Bucy features rather than apraxia. Preserved spontaneous use of objects is the key clue to ideomotor apraxia.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has headache and papilledema. MRI shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle. Where is the obstruction most likely located?
items.explanation: Dilation of the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle indicates obstruction at the aqueduct of Sylvius, a common site of noncommunicating hydrocephalus. Blockage of the outlet foramina would dilate the fourth ventricle too. Impaired absorption at arachnoid granulations gives communicating hydrocephalus with all ventricles enlarged. Foramen of Monro obstruction would affect one or both lateral ventricles but spare the third.

items.stem: In the classic model of basal ganglia circuitry, how does the direct pathway facilitate movement?
options: It excites the subthalamic nucleus, which excites the internal pallidum
It inhibits the thalamus, which reduces unwanted cortical output
It inhibits the internal globus pallidus, which disinhibits the thalamus
It excites the substantia nigra pars reticulata through the striatum
items.explanation: Striatal neurons of the direct pathway, expressing D1 receptors, inhibit the internal globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata, which normally inhibit the thalamus. The thalamus is therefore released to excite cortex. Excitation of the subthalamic nucleus belongs to the indirect pathway and increases inhibition of movement. Direct inhibition of the thalamus describes the pallidal output, not the direct pathway's effect.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman suffers a prolonged episode of severe hypotension after cardiac arrest. She develops marked bilateral proximal arm weakness with relatively preserved hand strength. Which territory is most likely injured?
options: Border zone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries
items.explanation: Global hypoperfusion injures the watershed areas first. The anterior and middle cerebral border zone lies over the motor strip's shoulder and arm region, producing the man-in-a-barrel pattern of proximal arm and leg weakness. Posterior cerebral injury would cause visual loss. Choroidal infarcts affect the internal capsule, and spinal artery infarcts produce cord syndromes with sensory loss.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man received a prolonged course of gentamicin for sepsis. He now reports that the world appears to bounce when he walks, and he is unsteady in the dark. Which abnormality best explains the bouncing vision?
options: Impaired smooth pursuit gain during slow target tracking
Reduced vestibulo-ocular reflex gain during head movement
Slowed saccade velocity during horizontal refixation
Bilateral abducens nerve paralysis from ototoxic injury
items.explanation: Aminoglycosides damage vestibular hair cells, so head rotation no longer produces an equal and opposite eye movement, and the image slips across the retina with every step, called oscillopsia. Pursuit and saccade circuits remain intact and are not the cause. Abducens palsy would cause horizontal diplopia and an esotropia rather than motion of the visual scene during walking. Bilateral loss is confirmed by abnormal head impulse tests.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has fluent comprehension and intact repetition but produces very little spontaneous speech, answering only after long delays. He repeats long sentences perfectly. Which lesion is most likely?
options: Left posterior superior temporal gyrus with arcuate fasciculus injury
Left angular gyrus adjacent to the occipital pole
Left inferior temporal cortex adjacent to the fusiform gyrus
Left frontal cortex anterior and superior to the Broca area
items.explanation: Reduced spontaneous output with preserved comprehension and repetition is transcortical motor aphasia, caused by injury to frontal regions such as the supplementary motor area or the cortex anterior and superior to Broca, often in anterior watershed infarcts. Arcuate injury impairs repetition. An angular lesion causes alexia and agraphia. Inferior temporal injury causes naming difficulty or visual agnosia, not reduced output.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man develops perioral numbness, vomiting, and ascending weakness shortly after eating improperly prepared pufferfish. Which structure does the toxin block?
options: Voltage-gated potassium channels that repolarize the axon
Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Presynaptic calcium channels at nerve terminals
items.explanation: Tetrodotoxin binds the outer pore of voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing the rapid depolarization that generates action potentials, so numbness and paralysis follow. Potassium channels mediate repolarization, and blocking them would prolong, not abolish, firing. Nicotinic receptor blockade is the mechanism of curare, and presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome rather than acute toxin exposure.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man on aspirin develops confusion and mild left hemiparesis three weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the right hemisphere. Which vessels were most likely torn?
options: Bridging veins crossing the subdural space to the dural sinuses
Middle meningeal artery branches within the epidural space
Lenticulostriate arteries within the basal ganglia
Penetrating branches of the anterior cerebral arteries
items.explanation: A crescent collection that crosses suture lines and develops after minor trauma in an older adult reflects a subdural hematoma, from tearing of bridging veins as the atrophic brain moves within the skull. Epidural hematomas arise from the middle meningeal artery and have a lens shape. Lenticulostriate and anterior cerebral penetrators cause deep intracerebral hemorrhage, not extra-axial collections.

items.stem: A physiology tutorial asks why a neuron cannot fire a second action potential immediately after the first, no matter how strong the stimulus. What is the explanation?
options: Potassium channels remain closed and block repolarization during the spike
The sodium-potassium pump has depleted intracellular sodium during the spike
Sodium channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes
Calcium influx at the terminal blocks further axonal depolarization
items.explanation: During the absolute refractory period, the inactivation gates of voltage-gated sodium channels are closed, so no stimulus can open them until the membrane repolarizes. This ensures unidirectional propagation. Potassium channels open, rather than stay closed, during repolarization. The pump restores gradients slowly and is not responsible for the refractory state. Terminal calcium influx triggers transmitter release.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body. He also has a small left pupil with ptosis. Which lesion explains the pupil finding?
options: Descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral medulla
Oculomotor nerve fascicle in the midbrain
Medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons
items.explanation: This is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome. The hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers descend through the lateral medulla, so injury causes ipsilateral Horner syndrome with miosis and ptosis. The Edinger-Westphal nucleus and oculomotor fascicle lesions would produce a large pupil, not a small one. The medial longitudinal fasciculus mediates conjugate gaze and does not carry pupillary sympathetic fibers.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has sudden right hemiparesis sparing the face, loss of vibration and position sense on the right, and tongue deviation to the left on protrusion. Which artery is most likely occluded?
options: Anterior spinal artery branch to the medulla
items.explanation: Contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face, contralateral loss of medial lemniscus sensation, and ipsilateral tongue weakness make up the medial medullary syndrome, caused by pyramidal, lemniscal, and hypoglossal involvement from occlusion of anterior spinal or vertebral branches. The posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral medulla. The anterior inferior and superior cerebellar arteries supply the pons and rostral cerebellum.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has weakness of the left lower face after a right hemispheric stroke, but she wrinkles her forehead symmetrically. Which mechanism explains the forehead sparing?
options: Upper facial motor neurons are innervated by the trigeminal nerve
Frontalis fibers leave the facial nucleus through the abducens nerve
Corticobulbar fibers to the forehead remain uncrossed in the medulla
Upper facial motor neurons receive bilateral corticobulbar input
items.explanation: The part of the facial nucleus serving the forehead receives both crossed and uncrossed corticobulbar fibers, so a unilateral hemispheric lesion spares the forehead, whereas the lower face receives mainly contralateral input. A nuclear or nerve lesion, as in Bell palsy, would involve the forehead too. The trigeminal and abducens nerves do not innervate frontalis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman receives botulinum toxin injections for cervical dystonia. At the cellular level, which proteins does the toxin cleave to produce its effect?
items.explanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins such as SNAP-25 or synaptobrevin, preventing synaptic vesicles from fusing with the presynaptic membrane, so acetylcholine release stops and the injected muscle weakens. The toxin does not damage calcium channels, which are the target in Lambert-Eaton syndrome. It leaves acetylcholinesterase intact, unlike organophosphates, and spares the postsynaptic receptors that are attacked in myasthenia gravis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a pituitary stalk tumor and sustained fever of 39.5 C with absent sweating and no infection. Which hypothalamic area is most likely damaged?
items.explanation: The anterior hypothalamus contains the preoptic area that senses warming and triggers sweating and vasodilation, so its destruction produces hyperthermia. The posterior hypothalamus drives heat conservation and shivering, so its injury causes hypothermia or poikilothermia. The lateral area controls feeding and arousal, and the suprachiasmatic nucleus sets circadian rhythm. Such central hyperthermia typically does not respond to antipyretic drugs.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has repeated episodes of transient painless loss of vision in the right eye that she describes as a curtain descending. Which vessel gives off the branch responsible for supplying the retina?
options: Posterior cerebral artery from the basilar artery
Ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid artery
Anterior communicating artery of the circle of Willis
Middle meningeal artery from the maxillary artery
items.explanation: The central retinal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, the first major branch of the internal carotid artery after the cavernous segment, so emboli from carotid plaque cause amaurosis fugax. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital cortex, and its occlusion causes a homonymous field defect. The anterior communicating artery connects the anterior cerebral arteries, and the middle meningeal artery supplies dura.

items.stem: A neurology resident reviews vestibular physiology with a 23-year-old man whose head is turned quickly to the right. What happens to the afferent firing of the vestibular nerves?
options: Decreases on the right horizontal canal and increases on the left
Increases equally on both horizontal canals
Increases on the right horizontal canal and decreases on the left
Decreases equally on both horizontal canals
items.explanation: Head rotation to the right deflects hair cells in the right horizontal canal toward the kinocilium, which depolarizes them and raises afferent firing, while the left canal is inhibited. The difference in tonic firing between sides drives the reflex that moves the eyes slowly to the left. A symmetric change would not signal rotation, and the reverse pattern would describe a leftward turn.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has damage to the structure that relays auditory information from the inferior colliculus to the primary auditory cortex. Which structure is this?
items.explanation: The medial geniculate nucleus receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium and projects through the auditory radiation to Heschl gyrus. The lateral geniculate nucleus relays optic tract fibers to the calcarine cortex, and the ventral posteromedial nucleus relays facial somatosensation and taste. The pulvinar is a large associative nucleus involved in visual attention.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman asks why a lumbar puncture performed at the L3-L4 interspace is safe in adults. Which anatomic fact answers her question?
options: The adult spinal cord ends near L1 to L2, below which only roots remain
The adult spinal cord ends near L4, and the dura is thick below that point
The subarachnoid space ends at L1, so the needle enters the epidural space only
The conus medullaris lies at S2 and is protected by the sacral vertebrae
items.explanation: In adults the conus medullaris usually ends at the L1-L2 level, while the subarachnoid space continues to S2 and holds the cauda equina roots, which float away from the needle. A needle at L3-L4, found at the level of the iliac crests, can therefore sample CSF with little risk of cord injury. The cord reaches L3 only in newborns, and it never ends at S2.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has morning vomiting and wide-based gait. He sways when sitting unsupported but has normal finger-to-nose testing. Imaging shows a midline posterior fossa mass. Which cerebellar region is primarily involved?
items.explanation: Truncal ataxia with preserved limb coordination localizes to the midline vermis, which controls axial and gait function. Hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral appendicular dysmetria and intention tremor, which are absent here. An isolated flocculonodular lesion would emphasize vestibular signs and nystagmus. The dentate nucleus is the main output pathway of the hemispheres and would produce limb ataxia.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy with a midline vermian tumor is evaluated. Which deep cerebellar nucleus receives the main output from the Purkinje cells of the vermis?
items.explanation: Purkinje cells of the vermis project to the fastigial nucleus, which in turn influences vestibular and reticular nuclei to control posture, gait, and axial muscles. The dentate nucleus receives the lateral hemisphere and sends fibers to the ventrolateral thalamus and red nucleus. The emboliform and globose nuclei, together the interposed nuclei, receive paravermian output and regulate limb movement.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has vertical diplopia after a motorcycle collision. It is worst when looking down and toward the nose, and he tilts his head away from the affected side. Which feature is unique to the nerve involved?
options: It exits the skull through the superior orbital fissure with the ophthalmic artery
It leaves the brainstem dorsally and innervates the contralateral muscle
It carries parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil
It runs between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
items.explanation: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem, and its fibers decussate so the nucleus innervates the contralateral superior oblique. It has the longest intracranial course and is vulnerable to head trauma. Parasympathetic pupil fibers belong to the oculomotor nerve, which also passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has progressive magnetic gait, urinary urgency, and slowed thinking over a year. MRI shows enlarged ventricles with tight high-convexity sulci. Which process best explains the ventricular enlargement?
options: Obstruction of flow through the cerebral aqueduct
Overproduction of fluid by a choroid plexus papilloma
Reduced CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
Ex vacuo expansion from diffuse cortical neuronal loss
items.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus in which impaired absorption of CSF, often after prior hemorrhage or meningitis, enlarges all ventricles without a mechanical block. Aqueductal obstruction would spare the fourth ventricle. Choroid plexus papilloma is rare and typically affects children. Ex vacuo enlargement from atrophy is accompanied by widened sulci rather than the tight high-convexity sulci shown here.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man with status epilepticus receives intravenous lorazepam. Which molecular action produces its anticonvulsant effect?
options: Increased duration of chloride channel opening at the GABA-A receptor
Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in a use-dependent manner
Inhibition of the glutamate NMDA receptor ion channel
Increased frequency of chloride channel opening at the GABA-A receptor
items.explanation: Benzodiazepines bind between alpha and gamma subunits of the GABA-A receptor and increase how often the chloride channel opens when GABA is present, causing hyperpolarization. Barbiturates instead lengthen channel open time, which is why they can act without GABA at high doses. Sodium channel blockade describes phenytoin and carbamazepine, and NMDA channel blockade describes ketamine and memantine.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman cannot look to the right with either eye. Passive turning of the head to the left does not move the eyes to the right, and she has right facial weakness. Which lesion is most likely?
items.explanation: The abducens nucleus contains both motor neurons for the lateral rectus and interneurons projecting through the contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus, so a nuclear lesion causes ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy that the vestibulo-ocular reflex cannot overcome. A frontal eye field lesion, in contrast, is overcome by reflex testing. Left fasciculus injury causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and the oculomotor nucleus controls adduction rather than abduction. Facial weakness reflects the nearby facial fascicle.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has bilateral loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders and arms in a cape distribution, with preserved vibration and position sense and normal strength early on. Which structure is first damaged by the cervical lesion?
options: Lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus
Fasciculus gracilis in the posterior funiculus
Dorsal spinocerebellar tract in the lateral funiculus
Decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure
items.explanation: Pain and temperature fibers cross in the anterior white commissure near the central canal within a few segments of entry, so an expanding central cavity, as in syringomyelia, interrupts them bilaterally at the level of the cavity, producing a cape distribution. Vibration and proprioception travel in the dorsal columns and are spared. Corticospinal weakness appears later, and spinocerebellar tract injury produces ataxia.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a cerebellar tumor has severe ipsilateral limb ataxia. Which structure carries the main afferent input from the contralateral pons to the cerebellum?
items.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle is the largest and carries only afferents: crossed corticopontocerebellar fibers from the pontine nuclei. The superior peduncle carries most efferents to the red nucleus and thalamus, and the inferior carries spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar input from the cord and medulla. The cerebral peduncle is a midbrain structure containing descending corticofugal tracts, not a cerebellar connection.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man with a foramen magnum meningioma has weakness of both arms with relative sparing of the legs, and he cannot raise his arms. Which pathway is most affected?
options: Decussating corticospinal fibers for the arms at the cervicomedullary junction
Uncrossed lateral corticospinal fibers in the thoracic cord
Posterior columns carrying proprioception in the cervical cord
Spinothalamic fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure
items.explanation: At the pyramidal decussation, arm fibers cross rostral to the leg fibers, so a lesion at the cervicomedullary junction produces bilateral arm weakness with leg sparing, called cruciate paralysis. Thoracic corticospinal injury would affect the legs, not the arms. Dorsal column loss would cause sensory ataxia, and spinothalamic injury would cause loss of pain and temperature without paralysis.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has neck pain radiating to the lateral forearm and thumb, thumb numbness, and weakness of elbow flexion with a reduced biceps reflex. Which root is most likely compressed?
items.explanation: The C6 root supplies the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, elbow flexion and wrist extension, and sensation over the lateral forearm and thumb. A C5 radiculopathy causes shoulder abduction weakness and lateral upper arm numbness. C7 affects triceps strength, the triceps reflex, and the middle finger. C8 involves finger flexors, intrinsic hand muscles, and the little finger.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman receiving cisplatin has intractable vomiting despite a drug that barely penetrates the brain. Which anatomic feature explains the vomiting?
options: Tight junctions are absent throughout the cerebral cortex
Astrocyte endfeet are absent around the cerebral arteries
The choroid plexus capillaries have tight endothelial junctions
The area postrema lacks a blood-brain barrier
items.explanation: The area postrema, a circumventricular organ in the floor of the fourth ventricle, has fenestrated capillaries and no blood-brain barrier, so circulating emetogenic drugs can stimulate its chemoreceptor trigger zone. Cortical capillaries retain tight junctions. Astrocyte endfeet are present around cerebral vessels. Choroid plexus capillaries are fenestrated, and the blood-CSF barrier is formed by the epithelial cells instead.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman after a bilateral posterior cerebral artery infarct insists she can see well, yet she walks into furniture and confidently describes the room incorrectly. Pupillary light responses are normal. Which structures are damaged?
items.explanation: Cortical blindness with denial of the deficit and confabulation is Anton syndrome, caused by bilateral occipital injury, often from top of the basilar or posterior cerebral occlusion. Pupillary reflexes are preserved because the pretectal pathway lies upstream of the cortex. Optic nerve disease would abolish pupillary light responses. Geniculate lesions are rare, and parietal injury causes optic ataxia and simultanagnosia.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man is stabbed in the back. He has right leg weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception on the right, with loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left below the nipple line. What is the mechanism of the contralateral pain loss?
options: Spinothalamic fibers cross in the medulla
Spinothalamic fibers cross within a few segments of entry
Dorsal column fibers cross in the cord
Corticospinal fibers cross in the lower cord
items.explanation: This is a right hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome). Pain and temperature fibers enter, synapse, and cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments, so a hemisection spares the contralateral side's input and impairs the opposite side. Dorsal columns and corticospinal fibers cross in the medulla, so their loss is ipsilateral below the lesion.

items.stem: A 53-year-old man has anterograde amnesia after surgery near the third ventricle that interrupted the main efferent bundle from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies. Which structure was divided?
items.explanation: The fornix arches from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies within the Papez circuit, and its transection causes severe anterograde memory loss. The cingulum links the cingulate gyrus to the entorhinal region, closing the circuit. The stria terminalis connects the amygdala to the hypothalamus. The mammillothalamic tract links the mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamus, which is downstream of the fornix.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has loss of vibration and joint position sense in both feet, but normal sensation in the hands, from a cervical midline posterior cord lesion. Which tract is the most selectively affected?
items.explanation: The fasciculus gracilis lies medially in the posterior columns and carries proprioception and vibration from the legs and lower trunk, whereas the fasciculus cuneatus lies laterally and carries those modalities from the arms. The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature from the opposite body, and the dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries unconscious limb position information to the cerebellum.

items.stem: A developmental biology lecture asks which of the following structures arises from the neural crest. What is the correct answer?
options: Motor neurons of the anterior horn
Ependymal cells lining the central canal
items.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate from the border of the neural folds and give rise to dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, and melanocytes. Oligodendrocytes, anterior horn motor neurons, and ependymal cells all arise from the neural tube itself, the neuroectoderm. Crest-derived Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons, while oligodendrocytes myelinate central axons. Neural crest defects also cause conditions such as Hirschsprung disease.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a lesion of the right trigeminal sensory root. Which result is expected when the examiner touches the right cornea with a wisp of cotton?
options: Blink of the left eye only, with the right eye closing weakly
Blink of both eyes with a delayed response on the left
Blink of the right eye only, with a strong consensual response
items.explanation: The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and the efferent limb is the facial nerve to orbicularis oculi on both sides. A right afferent lesion therefore abolishes the blink in both eyes when the right cornea is stimulated, while touching the left cornea elicits a normal bilateral blink. A facial nerve lesion would spare consensual blink in the opposite eye.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has a stroke followed by contralateral hemibody numbness. Weeks later she develops severe burning pain on the same side, worsened by light touch. Which nucleus was most likely involved in the original infarct?
options: Ventral anterior nucleus of the thalamus
Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
items.explanation: Contralateral hemisensory loss followed by central pain describes the Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, from injury to the ventral posterolateral nucleus, which relays body somatosensation to the cortex. The ventral anterior nucleus relays basal ganglia output to motor areas. The lateral geniculate nucleus carries vision, and the anterior nucleus is part of the limbic circuit of Papez. Central pain arises from deafferentation and hyperexcitability of thalamocortical circuits.
